<reason>B more convincingly distinguishes connectivity’s benefits from whether expansion subsidies justify their lifetime costs and opportunity costs. A supplies plausible benefits and useful safeguards, but never adequately answers why procurement discipline establishes spending priority. B’s conditional willingness to fund justified projects does not establish A’s explicitly asserted pro-subsidy default. A also weakens its credibility by repeatedly attributing permanent market failure to B and claiming B refused to specify an acceptable metric before B’s answering turn occurred.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B sharply exploits A’s restriction of alternative-spending comparisons to “the same communities”: national funding requires counting benefits forgone elsewhere too. Coupled with the distinction between disciplining bids and justifying purchases, this leaves an allocation challenge that A’s closing does not resolve.</best_rebuttal>
